Clinical trial report: three treatments for anxiety

Día 4 · Bloque 2 — Ejercicio 3 (SOLUCIONES)

Author

Filip Andras - CIMCYC, Universidad de Granada

Published

October 15, 2026

Introduction

A randomised clinical trial compared two treatments for anxiety, cognitive-behavioural therapy (CBT) and pharmacological treatment, against a control group. Anxiety was measured with the Beck Anxiety Inventory (BAI) (Beck et al., 1988) before and after treatment. This report describes the sample, visualises the change and tests whether the change in anxiety depends on the treatment.

NoteSynthetic data

The data are synthetic: they were simulated for the course Introducción a la programación y análisis de datos en R (CIMCYC, Universidad de Granada) to practise the full workflow, from data to report. No real patients took part, and no clinical conclusion should be drawn from the results.

Data

All analyses were run in R (R Core Team, 2026), using RStudio (Posit team, 2026) as the development environment, with the packages afex (Singmann et al., 2025), emmeans (Lenth & Piaskowski, 2026), ggplot2 (Wickham, 2016) and gtsummary (Sjoberg et al., 2021); the versions are listed in the session information at the end.

The trial included 300 patients, allocated to three groups of 100, 100 and 100 patients (CBT, control, pharmacological). Table 1 summarises the sample before and after treatment.

Table 1: the sample by group

Figure 1: anxiety before and after treatment

As Figure 1 shows, the three groups are similar before treatment; afterwards, the control group remains above the two treated groups.

Analysis: does the change in anxiety depend on the treatment?

The model

The design has one between-subjects factor (group: CBT, pharmacological, control) and one within-subjects factor (time: before vs. after), so the question is a mixed ANOVA (Day 3): the effect of interest is the group × time interaction, i.e. whether the change from before to after differs between groups.


Univariate Type III Repeated-Measures ANOVA Assuming Sphericity

Assumptions

Figure 2 shows residuals that are close to normal, with a slightly short lower tail, and no pattern that would question the model. Sphericity is not an issue with only two levels of the within-subjects factor (a single difference, after − before).

Results

Anxiety decreased from before to after treatment overall, main effect of time: F(1, 297) = 788.06, p <0.001, η²g = 0.22; and the groups differed on average, main effect of group: F(2, 297) = 29.99, p <0.001, η²g = 0.15. Crucially, the group × time interaction was significant, F(2, 297) = 138.91, p <0.001, η²g = 0.09: the change in anxiety depended on the treatment.

Every number in that sentence is inline code that indexes tabla_mixto with [row, column]; it is written by hand because, unlike the correlation and the t-test (Day 3), a mixed ANOVA cannot yet be reported automatically with easystats::report(). To unpack the interaction, Table 2 reports the before − after change within each group (simple effects of time), and Table 3 compares the three groups at each time point, before and after treatment; both with the Holm correction (Holm, 1979).

Anxiety fell by 4.3 points in the CBT group and by 2.9 points in the pharmacological group, against 0.6 points in the control group (Table 2). Before treatment, no group differed from another; after treatment, all three pairwise differences were significant (Table 3).

Conclusion

After treatment, mean anxiety was 10.8 points in the CBT group, 12.7 in the pharmacological group and 15.2 in the control group. Both treatments reduced anxiety more than the control condition did, CBT somewhat more than medication, as the group × time interaction shows; the three-month follow-up is not yet included in this report.
